draft_context.source_title: Samsung Redefines Laundry With New A-70% and 13 Kg Bespoke AI Washers at IFA 2026
draft_context.description: *For illustrative purposes only. Product design and specifications are subject to change. Samsung Electronics today announced that it will showcase two new Bespoke AI Washer models during IFA 2026: 1 a 10 kg model designed to deliver A-70% energy efficiency 2 and a 13 kg large-capacity model engineered to fit within a standard 600 mm depth. As the official main sponsor of the IFA Creator Hub, Samsung will showcase its latest innovations at Humboldt Carré in Berlin, Germany from Sept. 2-6. The new Bespoke AI Washers will be among the products on display, highlighting Samsung’s latest advances in technology. The two new models combine improved energy efficiency and greater capacity with space-efficient design and AI-powered fabric care to help consumers manage laundry more efficiently and conveniently. “At Samsung, we are continually challenging the traditional trade-offs between energy efficiency, capacity and convenience,” said Hyoung Min Park, VP and Head of the Customer Experience Team of the Digital Appliances (DA) Business at Samsung Electronics. “During IFA 2026, we’re demonstrating how innovation can help consumers save energy, handle larger loads and enjoy a more intelligent and convenient laundry experience.” Larger 10 Kg Bespoke AI Washer Brings New Efficiency Milestone The Bespoke AI Washer with A-70% energy efficiency marks a new step forward for Samsung, following the A-55% Bespoke AI Washer introduced at IFA 2024 and the A-65% model showcased at IFA 2025. The new washer will be designed to consume up to 70% less energy than the minimum energy efficiency requirement for a Class A rating in Europe, while increasing washing capacity from 9 kg 3 to 10 kg. By improving capacity and energy efficiency simultaneously, the new model builds on the company’s continued research into overcoming the traditional compromise between washing larger loads and reducing energy consumption. Samsung has achieved these gains through engineering improvements across key areas, including motor efficiency, thermal management, and wash-cycle design. Together, these technologies reduce electricity consumption while maintaining effective cleaning performance and everyday usability. 13 Kg Bespoke AI Washer Offers Increased Capacity With Standard-Depth Footprint Samsung will also showcase the new Bespoke AI Washer with large capacity, which brings a 13 kg washing capacity to a standard European design depth of 600 mm. Using SpaceMax technology, which creates more space inside to enhance the mechanical design and incorporate a larger drum without increasing the external dimensions, the washer increases internal volume while maintaining a compact 24-inch form factor. This space-efficient design allows users to wash larger loads, bedding, and bulkier items — while helping the appliance fit within common European kitchen, utility-room, and furniture configurations. The washer also incorporates Samsung’s mono-body design, creating a unified form designed to blend naturally into a wide range of interiors. A slim front frame reinforces its streamlined silhouette, while refined colors, materials, and finishes contribute to a clean, understated appearance. At the center of the interface is a large touch display visually integrated with the detergent compartment. From this display, users can intuitively access cycle controls, connected features, and personalized laundry services through SmartThings. 4 Auto Open Door Helps Keep the Washer Interior Fresh For added convenience, both washers feature Auto Open Door. Once a wash cycle is complete, the washer door opens gradually to help release residual moisture from inside the drum. By automatically ventilating the interior after a cycle, Auto Open Door helps keep the washer interior fresh between cycles. Together, the new A-70% and 13 kg Bespoke AI Washers reflect Samsung’s continued effort to challenge traditional laundry trade-offs. They deliver great capacity with lower energy consumption, making everyday laundry more intelligent and convenient. The Bespoke AI Washer models shown at IFA 2026 are development-stage display models. Specifications are subject to change, and commercial availability to be determined. ︎ Based on Samsung internal testing. The energy consumption of this Bespoke AI Washer [WF90*/24 (10kg)] achieves an EEI of 15.5 (15.3 kWh / 100 cycles), which is up to 70.2% more energy efficient compared to the minimum threshold for Class A (EEI 52 for 10 kg models) under Regulation (EU) No 2019/2014. Final testing to be conducted prior to EPREL registration. Results may vary depending on the usage environment. Energy ratings tested with the Eco 40–60 program. ︎ Compared to the previous model WF90H09C4S with A-65% energy efficiency and 9 kg washing capacity. ︎ Available on Android and iOS devices. A Wi-Fi connection and a Samsung account are required. ︎

draft_context.source_title: I tested Sony’s affordable Bravia 5 TV, and it offers a lot of punch for its price tag, throwing serious shade on Sony’s previous mid-range screens
draft_context.description: Sony Bravia 5: Two-minute review The Sony Bravia 5 is a mini-LED TV with crisp images, strong contrast and great gaming features. It occupies that level in Sony’s TV range where the brand has historically struggled to maintain its high standards. The Bravia 5, though, bucks this trend in pretty spectacular fashion. The Sony Bravia 5 retains both mini-LED lighting and local dimming, for starters, as well as an 120Hz panel to keep gamers happy. Sony says the Bravia 5 LCD panels are still made to the brand’s Master Backlight Drive standard too, and they’re equipped with a full up-to-date version of the Google TV smart system. There are ‘catches’ to this promising specification, of course. In particular, the Bravia 5 won’t benefit from as many dimming zones as the step up Bravia 7, or achieve so much brightness. In reality, though, the 65-inch Bravia 5 (AKA the K65XR55) delivers much less of a step down from Sony’s mid-range models than expected based on past Sony lines. Pictures are vibrant, crisp, full of contrast and just way less compromised than previous generations of the same level of Sony TV would have been. Add punchy, clean and detailed audio to its surprising picture talents, and the Bravia 5 is the Sony value TV we’ve always wanted. Sony Bravia 5 review: Price and release date The LG B6 delivers deep black tones and crisp textures (Image credit: Future) Release Date: July 2025 55-inch: $1,399.99 / £1,299 / AU$1,999 65-inch: $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 75-inch: $1,999.99 / £1,799 / AU$2,899 85-inch: $2,399.99 / £2,299 / AU$3,899 98-inch: $4,999.99 / £4,499 (around AU$8,570) While the Bravia 5 is affordable by Sony TV standards, $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 is no longer cheap for a 65-inch TV. The Bravia 5 retains much more of Sony’s mid-range — and even premium — TV DNA than expected based on similarly positioned models in previous Sony ranges, though. As a result, it has at least the potential to take a clear performance edge over more affordable rivals. Sony Bravia 5 review: Specs Screen type Backlight Master Drive VA mini-LED with local dimming Sizes available 55, 65, 75, 85 and 98 inches Refresh rate 120Hz Resolution 4K HDR support Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG Audio support 40W acoustic multi-audio speaker system featuring dual full-range (bass reflex) speakers and two ‘frame’ tweeters; Dolby Atmos and DTS:X decoding Smart TV Google TV (plus all main UK terrestrial broadcaster catch up apps for UK buyers) HDMI ports 4 (two full HDMI 2.1) Sony Bravia 5 review: Benchmark results Sony Bravia 5 review: Features (Image credit: Future) Mini-LED lighting Direct lighting with local dimming Bravia XR processor As I’ve hinted more than once already, the Sony Bravia 5 is packing much more feature heat than I would have expected it to, based on Sony TV ranges of the past. This is particularly true of the screen hardware at the Bravia 5’s heart. Designated one of Sony’s Master Backlight Drive panels, it is illuminated by mini-LEDs driven by a local dimming system that, according to my own counting efforts, operates across an impressive 240 zones. That’s 240 areas of the image that are capable of receiving their own light level, independent of their neighbors, according to the needs of the image. The Bravia 5’s panel is a VA type, too, which should further enhance contrast (though maybe not viewing angles). Meanwhile, even this far down Sony’s range, the brand's consistently impressive XR processor is still on hand to power all the constituent parts of the TV’s pictures. On top of this, rather than dropping down to 50/60Hz, the panel also maintains a native 120Hz refresh rate. Meanwhile, its support for high dynamic range images extends to Dolby Vision, as well as the more basic HDR10 and HLG formats. Sony is also unusual in the TV world for automatically applying an HDR upgrade to SDR sources on some of its picture presets. There’s no interest from Sony, though, in the HDR10+ format designed as an open-source alternative to Dolby Vision. The Bravia 5’s connections keep up with its step-up siblings. So you get four HDMIs (though only two support the TV’s full range of gaming features like VRR and ALLM), USB media playback support, and wireless support that includes Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.3, built-in Chromecast, Apple Airplay, and Apple HomeKit. (Image credit: Future) Sony’s TV business has long traded on its ‘from camera to TV’ product chain, and the potential for accuracy that this can bring. So as usual the Bravia 5’s Professional Mode setting, at least, will have been tuned alongside one of Sony’s professional mastering monitors, and the set is equipped with a bunch of so-called Calibrated modes designed to replicate as closely as possible the mastering standards of the Prime Video, Netflix and Sony Pictures Core video streaming services. Buying a Bravia 5 entitles you to 10 free films and 24 months of access to Sony Pictures Core too, by the way, complete with its unique high-bandwidth streaming speeds for enhanced picture quality. Further ‘third party’ endorsement finds the Bravia 5 earning an IMAX Enhanced badge, indicating that it has been deemed capable of doing justice to the special noise-limiting mastering processes and potential shifting aspect ratios associated with the IMAX Enhanced system. IMAX Enhanced titles are available on Sony Pictures Core and Disney+. The Bravia 5’s audio setup is pretty potent by mid-range TV standards. It offers two full range Bass Reflex-design drivers and two separated tweeters getting 10W a piece to deliver both Dolby Atmos and DTS:X soundtracks — the latter even includes the special tweaked version of DTS:X associated with IMAX Enhanced content. Features score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Picture quality Impressive brightness and light control Bold but also natural colour Genuine 4K sharpness and excellent 4K upscaling The Sony Bravia 5’s image quality instantly changes the fortunes of this level of Sony’s TV range, leaning much more towards the Sony TVs above it than those below. Particularly great to see is how much contrast the Bravia 5 retains for this level of Sony’s range. Black colors look deep and strikingly consistent, exhibiting minimal issues with backlight blooming around bright objects or general areas of clouding. That's despite the fact the screen is capable of hitting nearly 900 nit brightness peaks on a 10% HDR window and sustaining an OLED-beating 595 nits with a full 100% HDR window. Combining Sony’s backlight structure and XR Processor, the Bravia 5 can maintain more intensely bright highlights against dark backdrops than you’d expect for its price tag, despite how limited the clouding around such highlights is. This combination of bright stand-out objects and limited clouding is very difficult to achieve with locally dimmed TVs, yet the Bravia 5 makes it look easy. Dark scenes look stable, too, in the sense that you never feel aware of the sudden brightness jumps or obvious ‘handovers’ between different dimming zones as bright objects move around a dark backdrop. (Image credit: Future) Many screens with strong contrast performances are often capable of good color reproduction too — and this trend continues with the Bravia 5. In its Standard preset, it produces strikingly vibrant, rich and bold tones (actually upgraded to HDR if you’re watching an SDR source) that still feel balanced, full of subtlety and nuance, and connected to source tones for the most part. They feel more like amplifications of source content colors rather than aggressive departures from them. Unfortunately, the Bravia 5 pushes this amplification effect way too far in the Vivid preset, which is best avoided. But the Standard setting is an excellent bright room option, as well as actually being delicate and balanced enough to hold up as a dark room movie night option if your image tastes tend towards the bright and vibrant. Unlike most other TV brands, Sony doesn't offer a Filmmaker Mode preset for AV fans who favor ‘as the director intended’ viewing. Its Professional Mode, though, does pretty much the same thing, with an emphasis on trying to match the image as closely as possible to Sony’s professional video mastering monitor. Using Portrait Display’s Calman Ultimate software, G1 signal generator and C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, the accuracy of the Bravia 5 Professional mode was easy enough to demonstate. Errors recorded in both SDR and HDR across the board came in at well under the 3.0 DeltaE 2000 average beyond which errors might become visible to the human eye. (Image credit: Future) The Bravia 5’s Professional mode doesn’t just measure well. It also looks subjectively lovely, packed with the subtle texturing, immaculate color balance, and remarkable light control for a lower mid-range LCD TV. The benefits of Sony finally being able to introduce a superior core panel in a TV at the Bravia 5’s level are arguably at their most obvious in the Professional preset, in fact, given that this mode uses relatively few processing tools to help ‘boost’ its appearance. Inevitably, given it’s far from the most premium TV in Sony’s range, there are a few limitations to the Bravia 5’s picture performance. Dark scenes in the Professional mode look a little grayer than they do in Standard mode, and backlight blooming around bright objects can become more noticeable if you view the TV from an angle. Strangely, certain shades of red can look a bit over-ripe during dark scenes, and some dark shots also take on a slightly green undertone. Finally, some of Sony’s preset choices don’t actually help the Bravia 5’s pictures at all. Motion processing only really helps 24p movie sources if it’s switched to its True Cinema mode, for instance, with other settings tending to generate unwanted digital side effects or leave the image looking unnaturally smooth. I’d also recommend turning off the noise reduction features, especially with native 4K sources, to ensure the screen’s impressive native sharpness isn’t unnecessarily softened away. The Bravia 5’s issues are mild enough or easy enough to fix, though, that they don’t stop it from being an all-round excellent picture performer for its money. Picture quality score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Sound quality (Image credit: Future) Impressive clarity and detailing Sound doesn’t suffer with distortions Bass is a bit lightweight The Bravia 5’s sound joins its pictures in being impressively expressive and clean, working within the speaker’s limitations rather than pushing things beyond their breaking point as so many integrated TV sound systems are wont to do. Even the brightest, shrillest treble sounds are produced without sounding thin or brittle, while the mid-range is clean and pretty expansive, able to cope with the ebbs and flows of even quite dense action scenes without sounding forced, muddy or compressed. It uses its four-speaker system well to create a fairly large soundstage, too — one that’s well populated with accurately placed, crisp but never overstated details. My only complaint is that the Bravia 5 feels a bit light in the bass department. Dinosaur footprints, rumbling space ships, meaty explosions and the like don’t hit with quite as much heft as I’d like. At the same time, though, not even Hollywood’s most extreme bass moments cause the Bravia 5’s speakers to succumb to distracting crackles or distortions. Sound quality score: 4 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Design (Image credit: Future) Multi-point foot attachment Recycled plastic remote control Minimal frame The Bravia 5’s design doesn’t feel like much of a step-down at all from Sony’s Bravia 7 series. Its screen frame is extremely narrow, distracting scarcely at all from the pictures within, and it also stays fairly trim around the back for a lower mid-range LCD TV. Its feet look a little basic when attached to such an elegantly minimalistic screen, perhaps. But Sony has thoughtfully provided the option to attach them either quite close together or out towards the TV’s bottom corners, depending on the width of the furniture you want to stand the TV on. Build quality is good, too, and despite its relatively affordable position in Sony’s current TV range, it ships with two remote controls. The sleeker, more modern and more feature-rich handset is made largely made from recycled plastic, as part of Sony’s wide-ranging attempts to make the TV production process greener. Design score: 4 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Smart TV & menus LG's webOS 26 is easily one of the best smart TV platforms around (Image credit: Future) Google TV smart system YouView for full UK app coverage Optional Bravia Cam The Sony Bravia 5 runs the latest Google TV system very well, avoiding the sluggishness the system sometimes causes on less powerful TVs. Google TV carries pretty much all of the most popular and important video streaming services, and Sony has helpfully worked round Google TV’s blind spot when it comes to some of the UK’s most popular terrestrial broadcaster catch up services by adding the YouView app. Google TV can still feel a little overwhelming in its presentation and doesn’t feel as intelligent as some rival smart systems when it comes to recommending content based on your viewing habits. The smarter of the two remote controls Sony provides, though, makes navigation of the menus feel straightforward. On top of this, you can access a good range of features and issue quite complex search instructions just by talking to the Bravia 5 via the Google Assistant voice recognition system. You can even add basic gesture control features to the Bravia 5 if you cough up £200 for one of Sony’s Bravia Cam accessories. This add-on camera can also detect your location in the room and adjust the TV’s picture and sound settings accordingly, as well as issuing audio warnings if it detects anyone getting too close to the screen. I’m not personally convinced Bravia CAM does enough to justify its price, but if the features I’ve just described sound good to you, then fill your boots! Smart TV & menus score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Gaming (Image credit: Future) 4K/120Hz support VRR support Perfect For PlayStation 5 support The Sony Bravia 5 is fairly, rather than brilliantly, well specified as a gaming display. For instance, while it does support 4K game feeds at 120Hz refresh rates, it only does so over two of its HDMIs, rather than all four. It also doesn’t stretch the refresh rate support to 144Hz or even 165Hz, like some rival TVs currently do. Similarly, while the Bravia 5 supports variable refresh rates, that support doesn’t extend to the AMD Freesync or Nvidia G-Sync systems. There is support for auto low latency mode switching, though, so the TV can automatically switch into its fastest responding picture mode when a game source is detected. While in this mode, the Bravia 5 takes just 13.3ms to render 60Hz gaming feeds. There’s support, too, for Sony’s unique Perfect For PlayStation 5 features, comprising a PS5-specific version of automatic game mode switching, and an excellent system where a connected PS5 is able to tell which Sony TV model it’s attached to, and automatically optimize its HDR output accordingly. You can also call up a dedicated gaming menu when the Bravia 5 is in Game mode, containing information on the game feed and a few helpful gaming assistants. Finally, the actual gaming experience when using one of the two wide-bandwidth HDMIs is very enjoyable. The TV’s vibrant, exceptionally sharp and contrast-rich pictures provide a perfect fit for today’s usually HDR and 4K graphics, while the rapid response time and VRR support means gaming never feels sluggish or laggy. Gaming score: 4 / 5 (Image credit: Future) Sony Bravia 5 review: Value Not so long ago, spending $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 to get a 65-inch TV as good and feature rich as the Sony Bravia 5 would have felt like a great deal. Recently, though, TCL in particular has drastically shifted the TV value ‘window’, with its bright, vibrant and gaming-friendly 65-inch C7K currently going for just £779. The Bravia 5 does offer more precision and balance in its pictures than the TCL C7K, but the price gap is big enough to mean you may feel like holding out for a special offer on Sony’s model, or searching beyond the most popular electronics retailers for a better deal. Value score: 3.5 / 5 Should I buy the Sony Bravia 5? Sony Bravia 5 scorecard Attributes Notes Rating Features Aside from a few gaming limitations, the Bravia 5 is well featured for its money. 4.5 / 5 Picture quality Vibrant, bright, sharp and contrast rich pictures reveal the presence of more excellent Sony backlighting and video processing systems. 4.5 / 5 Sound quality While bass heads might wish for a bit more low frequency impact, the Bravia 5’s sound is clean, punchy, detailed and unusually well staged. 4 / 5 Design With its choice of foot position, elegantly minimalist frame, slender frame and strong build quality, the Bravia 5 looks premium enough to match its price. 4 / 5 Smart TV and menus Google TV runs stably and reasonably slickly on the Bravia 5, making it easy to access the huge array of content options it offers. The set up menus are well organised and graphically rich, too. 4.5 / 5 Gaming Only two HDMIs support the Bravia 5’s full array of gaming features, and those features don’t include absolutely everything some rivals offer. However, the exclusive to Sony TVs Auto HDR ‘Perfect For PlayStation 5’ feature is excellent, and the screen feels responsive and immersive. 4 / 5 Value While the Bravia 5 is well priced for a Sony TV that performs as well as this one, competition at this price level is brutal these days. 3.5 / 5 Buy it if... You want that Sony picture feel for less The Bravia 5 holds on to more of the panel and processing prowess of more premium Sony TVs than you'd expect at this price. You have a PlayStation 5 The Bravia 5’s Perfect For PlayStation 5 features allow a PS5 console to automatically feed it optimized HDR games — a genuinely helpful feature given that HDR gaming is still in something of a ‘wild west’ stage at the moment. You want to put your TV on a narrow piece of furniture While the widest foot placement looks more elegant, Sony provides the option to place the Bravia 5’s feet close together as well. Don't buy it if... You are on a tight budget Some rivals, most notably TCL, sell bright, vibrant 65-inch TVs with good gaming features for substantially less than the Bravia 5 costs. You have more than two premium gaming sources Only two of the Bravia 5’s HDMI ports support the full range of cutting-edge gaming features that today’s gamers are looking for (4K/120Hz and VRR). You want a Filmmaker Mode and/or HDR10+ support If you happen to be a real fan of Filmmaker Mode presets and the HDR10+ rival to Dolby Vision HDR, you should know that the Bravia 5 doesn’t support either of these features. Sony Bravia 5 review: also consider Sony Bravia 5 TCL C7K LG C5 Samsung QN90F Price (65-inch) $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 $899.99 / £779 / AU$2,295 $1,399.99 / £1,599 / AU$2,699.99 $1,599.99 / £1,399 / AU$2,899 Screen type Backlight Master Drive VA mini-LED with local dimming Mini-LED with local dimming WRGB OLED Mini-LED with local dimming Refresh rate 120Hz 4K 144Hz (up to 288Hz at lower resolution) 144Hz 120Hz (up to 165Hz with Motion Xcelerator technology) HDR support HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG HDR10, HDR10+, HLG Smart TV Google TV (plus all main UK terrestrial broadcaster catch up apps for UK buyers) Google TV with YouView WebOS 25 Tizen OS HDMI ports 4 (two full HDMI 2.1) 4 (two HDMI 2.1) 4 x HDMI 2.1 4 x HDMI 2.1 TCL C7K With its extreme brightness, surprisingly good backlight control and uncompromising gaming features, the C7K has single-handedly rewritten the TV value rulebook. While Sony’s set delivers a more controlled image, the C7K’s bang for your buck is crazy. And it supports all four key HDR formats too. Read our full TCL C7K review . LG C5 With LG’s 2026 OLED TV range just arriving, at the time of writing you can buy 2025’s C5 at a knock down price. Every pixel in OLED TVs delivers its own color and light without compromising its neighbors, delivering stunning contrast. The C5 also delivers excellent gaming support, and some of the most accurate pictures around. Read our full LG C5 OLED TV review. Samsung QN90F Samsung’s flagship 4K mini-LED TV for 2025 is also still around as we wait for the brand’s 2026 models, and it looks like strong value at its current $1,599.99 / £1,399 / AU$2,899 price. Its impressive pictures are joined by four full HDMI 2.1 ports, and an Object Tracking Sound (OTS) system that does a strikingly good job of placing sound effects in the right place on screen. Read our full Samsung QN90F TV review. How I tested the Sony Bravia 5 Tested over three weeks Tested with 4K Blu-rays, multiple streaming platforms and resolutions, Freeview HD broadcasts, and HD Blu-rays Reviewed in both dark and light dedicated test room conditions, on its feet in both corner and mid wall positions I tested the Sony Bravia 5 over a three-week period in a variety of room conditions — including using it as a regular living room TV for more than a week. I checked out streamed content at a variety of resolutions from all of the main video streaming platforms, including Sony’s exclusive Sony Pictures Core high-bandwidth services. I also watched tuner channels and fed it a selection of our regularly used test Blu-rays and 4K Blu-ray discs. Gaming was explored using a PlayStation 5, an Xbox Series X and a gaming PC. The Sony Bravia 5 retains both mini-LED lighting and local dimming, for starters, as well as an 120Hz panel to keep gamers happy. Sony says the Bravia 5 LCD panels are still made to the brand’s Master Backlight Drive standard too, and they’re equipped with a full up-to-date version of the Google TV smart system.

There are ‘catches’ to this promising specification, of course. In particular, the Bravia 5 won’t benefit from as many dimming zones as the step up Bravia 7, or achieve so much brightness. Pictures are vibrant, crisp, full of contrast and just way less compromised than previous generations of the same level of Sony TV would have been.

draft_context.source_title: 10 Years of MongoDB Atlas: Built for What’s Next
draft_context.description: Nearly a decade ago, I joined MongoDB as a Senior Product Manager to help build the company’s new cloud product, MongoDB Atlas. Our customers had been telling us they wanted to bring MongoDB’s familiar developer experience to the cloud, with the reliability and confidence teams needed to run in production. Atlas was our answer. Today, we’re celebrating 10 years of MongoDB Atlas, the generational data platform for AI applications, and the customers who pushed us to build it. Atlas was shaped in close conversation with those customers and scaled alongside them every step of the way. Today, more than 250,000 builders get started on Atlas every month. Atlas serves more than three trillion queries a day (a roughly threefold increase just since 2023!), and represents 75% of MongoDB’s revenue. Those numbers reflect something more important than growth: the trust builders and customers have placed in us to scale their businesses. That trust was earned by listening closely. Every major capability and architectural investment in Atlas was rooted in what customers asked for: the flexibility and speed of MongoDB’s document model, delivered in a platform that removed operational overhead and could scale with their applications. Over time, Atlas expanded beyond a managed database into a broader data platform, because builders kept asking for more flexibility, more simplicity, and more room to build. That matters even more in the AI era. AI applications create new demands, but the underlying requirement is familiar: builders need a platform that can support operational data, search, and retrieval while scaling through constant change—without forcing them to stitch together a mess of disconnected systems. We spent ten years becoming the flexible, durable data platform that builders trust. Those are the same qualities AI applications need most, and that’s why builders are now using Atlas to build trustworthy AI applications with highly accurate retrieval, real-time context, and the scale to run in production. Atlas 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Image 1 media Managed cloud databases become the default When Atlas launched in 2016, organizations were moving away from traditional data center build-outs and toward cloud-based delivery, a market Gartner forecasted would reach $204 billion (and is now approaching $1 trillion). Developers loved MongoDB as a flexible, intuitive foundation for building applications, but they also wanted to take advantage of the cloud. Atlas’s first promise was simple: bring MongoDB’s familiar developer experience to the cloud, with the reliability and confidence teams needed to run in production. Atlas 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Quote 1 aside To deliver that confidence to developer teams, we built Atlas with security, resilience, and performance at its core—from encryption and access controls to backups and high availability. The result was a service that teams could run in production with confidence, freeing developers to do their very best work without the headaches associated with database administration. By 2018, 81% of enterprises were operating in multi-cloud environments, and an IDG study found that more than half indicated they were thinking about cloud as a portfolio strategy. As customer architectures became more distributed, teams needed the flexibility to choose the cloud environment that fit their applications, teams, and compliance needs. To support them, we extended our original promise of simplicity into multi-cloud flexibility, with availability across all three major cloud providers. And in 2020, we introduced Atlas Multi-Cloud Clusters, making Atlas the first and only cloud database to let customers run applications simultaneously across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud regions—a unique achievement that gave organizations that require ultra-high availability one consistent data foundation across all the major clouds. Today, customers can run across over 125 AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure cloud regions, making Atlas the most widely available managed data platform in the world. Atlas 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Quote 2 aside Enterprises' scale, and consolidation becomes a customer priority As cloud adoption accelerated, customers wanted more than a hosted database. The cloud had become a long-term investment, and developers needed global reach, resilience, and a platform that could handle more workloads, securely, without requiring them to keep adding infrastructure around it. Because developers already trusted us on the fundamentals, Atlas could expand into the kinds of workloads enterprises could not afford to get wrong. For workloads like payments, inventory, and order processing, strong transactional consistency is a requirement. The addition of multi-document ACID transactions in 2018 brought that transactional consistency to MongoDB and marked an important step in MongoDB’s evolution, enabling MongoDB to serve the kinds of high-stakes transactional workloads that enterprises had historically reserved for relational databases. Now, customers could use MongoDB with greater confidence for a wider set of systems where accuracy, resilience, and trust could not be compromised. MongoDB extended its trustworthy database foundation with the launch of MongoDB Queryable Encryption, an industry-first encryption capability that allows customers to query encrypted data while keeping sensitive information protected when it is at rest, in transit, and in use—an important step for securing regulated and highly sensitive workloads. At the same time, Atlas continued to evolve to help customers operate at a larger scale. In 2020, we introduced Atlas Search and Online Archive, adding rich application search and giving customers a simpler, lower-cost way to store older data without losing easy access to it. In 2021, Native Time Series Collections and Live Resharding followed, helping customers manage time-stamped data more efficiently and scale architectures without downtime. These updates made Atlas easier for builders to work with as deployments became bigger, more distributed, and more complex, all while minimizing the number of disparate systems that development teams had to stitch together and maintain. Atlas 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Quote 3 aside Trustworthy AI becomes the new frontier Then, the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022—and with it the rise of generative AI—created a massive new challenge for builders. Enterprise adoption moved faster than standards and controls, leaving teams to figure out how to connect the necessary data components to run semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workloads together without creating a brittle mess of data pipelines, sync jobs, and specialized infrastructure that compromised security and performance. To help teams bring these critical AI building blocks together on one secure platform, Atlas evolved again. With the public release of Atlas Vector Search in 2023, MongoDB was one of the first databases to launch vector search as a native capability, which enabled developers to keep vectors close to operational data and run semantic retrieval directly in the database without having to manage a separate vector store. Search Nodes gave teams a way to scale search and vector workloads independently from the operational database, while Atlas Stream Processing gave builders a way to process real-time streaming data without adding separate infrastructure. The business demand for this architecture has been staggering: over 726,000 vector indexes and 55,000 vector applications have been created since we introduced Atlas Vector Search, and we’ve seen a 92% increase in customers showing production-level vector search usage over the past 12 months. And with the company’s acquisition of Voyage AI in 2025, MongoDB sharpened its focus on retrieval quality—bringing advanced embedding and reranking models into Atlas. The integration of Voyage AI was about rethinking the data architecture to help customers reduce hallucinations, improve relevance, and make AI useful in the real-world environments where accuracy and trust matter most. 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Quote 4 aside This immediately paid huge dividends for customers building highly accurate semantic search and RAG applications. But we knew that as the market moved towards autonomous AI, trustworthy retrieval and access to real-time context would matter even more. Agents and the future of the data layer Today, we’re firmly in AI’s agentic era. Builders want to deploy agents that can reason over business context with autonomy. But agent memory requires fast accuracy at scale so that the right information is recalled at precisely the right time. And this is where they run into a challenge. They're excited about agents, but they can't put an agent in front of their customers if the results are inconsistent, irrelevant, or flat-out wrong. That puts increasing focus on the data layer of the tech stack. Agents are only as good as the context they can retrieve, rank, and retain. If the underlying data is stale, incomplete, or poorly retrieved, the output will be wrong—regardless of how strong the model is. In practice, production agents depend less on model choice alone than on retrieval quality and the ability to ground responses in live operational data. With search, vector search, embeddings, and rerankers natively integrated into the Atlas platform, businesses are closing the gap between data and retrieval to produce fast, accurate results for agents at scale. And with foundational capabilities to ensure exceptional security, resilience, and performance, builders are freed up to do what they do best, instead of spending their days bogged down managing data infrastructure. Atlas 10 Year Anniversary Blog - Quote 5 aside Over the past decade, our goal has been to reduce operational burden for customers without compromising on the technical bar. As the industry moves toward agents, that aim still applies. We’re ten years in, and Atlas has grown into the data platform that runs intelligent, mission-critical applications for nearly 70,000 customers across every industry. The world runs on Atlas! Our customers pushed us to build everything that matters in the platform, so they could do more, faster. The same holds true today: the agentic AI era is raising the bar for innovation, and we're raising it with them. The ambition our customers bring to what they're building next is what drives us forward—and we're ready for it. Here's to the next 10 years.

draft_context.source_title: Ever wanted earbuds with a touchscreen case? Even if you haven’t, JBL's affordable Live Buds 4 are worth a look; think stellar sound and top features
draft_context.description: JBL Live Buds 4 review Ever wondered what life would be like if your earbuds had a touchscreen case? OK, you probably haven’t, but stick with me here. The JBL Live Buds 4 are the new generation of the audio specialist’s in-ears that pair with a smart charging case, enabling you to adjust sound settings, adapt ANC, and more — all without having to download a companion app. They’re a standout model in a congested market. The Live Buds 4 also sit within JBL's wider Live range, which is itself fairly congested in that it also includes the stemmed JBL Live Beam, plus the open-fit JBL Live Flex. This specific model, though — the Live Buds 4 — comes with a number of claimed upgrades over its predecessor, including enhanced ANC, new “fidelity drivers,” and boosted call quality. But are they worth the money and can they compete with options in our best earbuds roundup? Here’s what I think after three weeks of testing. We’ve got to start with the smart charging case, which has a revamped UI for a smoother, more complete user experience. The touchscreen is undoubtedly small, but it's highly responsive, and there are clear menus to access EQ tweaking, ANC modes, appearance options, and even tools like a flashlight and timer. I sometimes preferred using the JBL Headphones app for the ease of a larger screen, and the ability to set a custom wallpaper from my photo gallery, but for on-the-go tweaks, the charging case is a neat option — even if it is arguably a little bit gimmicky. But hey, I like a good gimmick now and then. Beyond what I’ve already mentioned, the case features a lot of fun features, like a smart-talk option, which picks up voices if you want to have a conversation while keeping your buds in. There are also customizable touch controls for the buds themselves (which I found to be reactive and convenient), and settings for how your voice sounds on a call, including a bright, natural, and powerful option. Speaking of calls, JBL has included 6 mics in these earbuds, as well as its new Perfect Calls 2.0 tech, which makes use of AI to keep your voice clear, even in noisier environments. As I mentioned in my JBL Live Beam 4 review (I know, it's easy to get confused with names), I did find my voice to be relatively clear on calls and when taking a recording, but unfortunately I didn’t get the premium clarity I was expecting. There was some noticeable sibilance in my recording, and I also found that some background noises remained more prominent than anticipated. I also want to talk about active noise cancellation, which has been improved for the Live 4 series. Overall, ANC is decent, but it’s still not up to the standards offered by buds from Apple and Bose. When out and about or on public transport, I could still make out background chatter, and in the office, typing sounds and doors closing were still audible. Sounds are still dulled effectively, and ANC is by no means bad — but if you’re expecting a curtain of silence when using the Live Buds 4, you may be left wanting more. (Image credit: Future) One area that the Buds 4 totally excel in, though, is sound quality. For earbuds in this price-range, the Buds 4 are excellent, dishing out impactful bass, clean mids, and expressive highs, impressive handling of dynamics, and good attention to detail. When tuning into Labor of Love by Ned Doheny, I was struck by the beautifully textured and weighted acoustic guitars, which were well separated from clear, tonally accurate vocals. Subtle percussive details also came through beautifully, and funky bass sounded impactful without drowning out other sounds across the frequency range. What’s more, by activating the higher-res Bluetooth codec, LDAC, I could make out some more intricacies in the mid-range, with almost life-like guitars taking the listening experience to the next level. The Live Buds 4 proved to cope brilliantly with any genre, though. With a deeper, more energetic track, such as Don’t Compare Yourself by Kolter, the pumping deep bass hit phenomenally hard, and reached down to tremendous depths for this level. Bassy synths sounded textured and controlled, lively drums sounded articulate and precise, and emotive vocals, while impactful, never overwhelmed the mix. I have very few complaints about the sound, and it’s super-simple to customize it to your liking with the EQ settings on the charging case or JBL headphones app. But one thing that could’ve been better was the spatial audio setting, which just lacked the clarity and openness of the standard tuning. I’d also argue that the soundstage is relatively broad on the Live Buds 4 anyway, so you should just keep this mode off if you ask me. (Image credit: Future) Let’s also talk design, as this is the main area where the Live Buds 4 differentiate themselves from the Beam and Flex. They take up a small, snug in-ear feel, which is ideal for those who prefer earbuds without the stems. I found the buds to be incredibly comfortable, and had no issue keeping them in for multiple hours at a time. They’re also highly secure, never feeling as if they’ll fall out of your ears. The buds also have a good standard of build, the case has an attractive, textured finish, and the model can be purchased in a wide range of colors. The buds are also IP55-rated, making them splashproof. Some rivals offer superior IP57 protection, but IP55 is enough to keep your buds safe on a rainy day. One more difference the Buds 4 have, is that they offer the least amount of battery life in the Live 4 lineup, with 8 hours of playtime with the buds when ANC is on, and up to 40 hours with the case. That’s still a good amount of playtime, and competes well with major rivals. So, are the JBL Live Buds 4 worth their £179.99 / AU$269.95 (about $240) asking price? For me, it’s an emphatic yes. Of course, they’re not the cheapest buds on the market, but they’re also a fair bit cheaper than big-name rivals like the AirPods Pro 3 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. They also sound fantastic for the money, with the nifty charging case only adding more value. Sure, they could do better in the call quality and ANC department, but ultimately, they still offer decent enough quality in those areas. (Image credit: Future) JBL Live Buds 4 review: price & release date List price of £179.99 / AU$269.95 (about $240) Revealed in May 2026 The JBL Live Buds 4 were revealed in May 2026, alongside their siblings, the JBL Live Beam 4 and the JBL Live Flex 4. They released about two years after their predecessor, the JBL Live Buds 3. They come in at £179.99 / AU$269.95 (about $240), which is the same as their predecessors cost at the point of launch (in the UK). We’re yet to catch wind of a release date and pricing for the US, but we’ll update this review accordingly if and when further details emerge. These buds are available at a relatively affordable price for the quality on offer, coming in at a lower cost than rivals such as the Apple AirPods Pro 3 and the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 . Our top pick for wireless earbuds whatever your budget is the Technics EAH-AZ100 , at $299 / £259 (around AU$478). So at quite a bit less than those figures, the JBL Live Buds 4 can be yours for a shade under flagship money — and that's a very good thing in terms of value. That said, the Huawei Freebuds Pro 5 are our current 'best mid-range' pick in that detailed guide, and those excellent buds retail for the same £179.99 fee as the JBL option. They don't have a smart charging case, but still, food for thought… JBL Live Buds 4 review: specs Drivers 10mm dynamic Active noise cancellation Yes Battery life 8 hours (buds, with ANC on); 10 hours (buds, with ANC off); 40 hours (with charging case) Weight 4.8g (per bud) Connectivity Bluetooth 6.0 Frequency range 20Hz-40kHz Waterproofing IP55 (Image credit: Future) Should I buy the JBL Live Buds 4? Attribute Notes Score Features Massive suite of features and neat smart case, but ANC and call quality could be better. 4/5 Sound quality Detailed, impactful, and rich audio, but spatial sound option in need of improvement. 4.5/5 Design Small and secure fit, strong standard of build, IP55-rated. 4.5/5 Value Great price for the sound and feature-rich case. 4.5/5 Buy them if… You want a more discreet in-ear look and feel Unlike the stemmed JBL Live Beam 4 and Flex 4, the Buds 4 have a low-key, ultra-compact in-ear look and feel. They’re more akin to models like the Bowers & Wilkins Pi8 in terms of build, and if you want compact and comfortable buds then they’re a top option. You’re digging the smart case There’s no doubt in my mind that a lot of people buy the Live series of earbuds for one reason, and one reason only: the smart charging case. Can I blame them? No. Is it a bit gimmicky? Sure. But do I like it? Yes, I genuinely do. You get quick access to all of the important features on the smart case, as well as tools like a torch and stopwatch, and it adds a bit of a fun factor to these great-sounding in-ears. Don’t buy them if… You want silence-inducing ANC Although JBL has improved the ANC in its latest batch of Live earbuds, the quality is still a bit middling in my view. You can get much better noise-cancelling from rivals like the AirPods Pro 3 . You’re looking for amazing spatial audio I didn’t find the spatial audio mode on the Live Buds 4 to be particularly effective, and preferred using them with this setting turned off. My go-to most days, the LG Tone Free T90S , have a great immersive listening mode, and even support Dolby Atmos. JBL Live Buds 4 review: also consider JBL Live Buds 4 Apple AirPods Pro 3 Huawei Freebuds Pro 5 Price £179.99 / AU$269.95 (about $240) $249 / £219 / AU$429 £179.99 (around $240; AU$270) Drivers 10mm dynamic Custom high excursion 11mm dynamic woofer and micro-planar tweeter Active noise cancellation Yes Yes Yes Battery life 8 hours (buds, with ANC on); 10 hours (buds, with ANC off); 40 hours (with charging case) 8 hours (buds, ANC on); 6.5 hours (buds, heart rate sensor on); 24 hours (case) 9 hours buds, 38 hours case Weight 4.8g (per bud) 5.6g (per bud) 5.5g (per bud) Connectivity Bluetooth 6.0 Bluetooth 5.3 Bluetooth 6.0 Frequency range 20Hz-40kHz Not stated 10Hz to 48kHz Waterproofing IP55 IP57 IP57 buds, IP54 case Apple AirPods Pro 3 If you want earbuds that are stylish, sound fantastic, supply stellar ANC and an iPhone will be your source device, look no further than the AirPods Pro 3 — if your budget will stretch to them We loved their comfortable, secure fit, new heart-rate monitor option, hearing health software and impressive waterproof rating, but they are still a little weak in the battery life department. Read our full Apple AirPods Pro 3 review for more. Huawei Freebuds Pro 5 Five-star svelte earbuds for the same money as the JBL set you came here to read about? Worth a look, surely — they're the model we recommend as the best mid-range buy in our dedicated earbuds buying guide. They might not be available if you happen to reside in the US, however, they're still worth shouting about to anyone else; the drivers are huge, the battery life is exceptional, the IP rating is a step up on most rivals, they're stuffed full of perks and the ANC is, as we said in our review, "excellent". Read all about them in our Huawei Freebuds Pro 5 review. How I tested the JBL Live Buds 4 (Image credit: Future) Tested over the course of three weeks Used in the office, on walks, and on public transport Mainly streamed tunes over Tidal, but tapped into Spotify too I spent three weeks putting the JBL Live Buds 4 through their paces. During this time, I listened to countless hours of music, messed around with everything the smart charging case had to offer, and exhausted their various features. As always, I made sure to use these buds in a range of environments — including at home or at the office, but also when out on walks near busy roads, and when on public transport like buses and trains. When listening to tunes, I predominantly streamed music over Tidal on my Xiaomi 17 phone, but I also jumped into Spotify now and then. I made sure to soft through the multi-genre TechRadar reference playlist , but also bumped a bunch of tunes from my personal library . More generally, I’ve spent years testing audio gear here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve reviewed everything from premium wireless headphones like the Sony 1000X The Collexion to hulking party speakers like the Marshall Bromley 750 . Of course, I’ve also tested many pairs of wireless earbuds, so I know exactly what it takes for a model to stand out in a highly competitive market. OK, you probably haven’t, but stick with me here. The JBL Live Buds 4 are the new generation of the audio specialist’s in-ears that pair with a smart charging case, enabling you to adjust sound settings, adapt ANC, and more — all without having to download a companion app.

They’re a standout model in a congested market. The Live Buds 4 also sit within JBL's wider Live range, which is itself fairly congested in that it also includes the stemmed JBL Live Beam, plus the open-fit JBL Live Flex. This specific model, though — the Live Buds 4 — comes with a number of claimed upgrades over its predecessor, including enhanced ANC, new “fidelity drivers,” and boosted call quality. But are they worth the money and can they compete with options in our best earbuds roundup? Here’s what I think after three weeks of testing.

We’ve got to start with the smart charging case, which has a revamped UI for a smoother, more complete user experience. The touchscreen is undoubtedly small, but it's highly responsive, and there are clear menus to access EQ tweaking, ANC modes, appearance options, and even tools like a flashlight and timer. I sometimes preferred using the JBL Headphones app for the ease of a larger screen, and the ability to set a custom wallpaper from my photo gallery, but for on-the-go tweaks, the charging case is a neat option — even if it is arguably a little bit gimmicky. But hey, I like a good gimmick now and then.

draft_context.source_title: AMD's Threadripper Halo is a local-AI workstation for researchers with deep pockets
draft_context.description: Machine learning researchers have a new and expensive option for doing local AI. AMD just raided its spare parts bin and cobbled together a DGX Station rival boasting up to 576 GB of HBM3e memory that it’s calling the Threadripper Halo. Announced at IFA 2026, the system, which is set to launch next year, marks the first time that AMD’s Instinct accelerators have been offered in a workstation form factor. But much like the AI Halo we reviewed earlier this year, the Threadripper Halo isn’t packing anything we haven’t seen before. The liquid-cooled system is powered by a 96-core Threadripper PRO 9995WX, which you may recall made its debut in 2025. The CPU is backed by up to 2 TB of DDR5 memory and up to 2.6 TB of combined system memory. As you probably already guessed, AMD is positioning the box as a local AI workstation for researchers. From what we gather, the system can be had with up to four of the company’s PCIe-based Instinct GPUs — though the systems displayed at IFA only showed two installed. Launched back in May, the MI350P is essentially half of an MI350X that’s been crammed into a PCIe form factor. Each accelerator packs 144 GB of speedy HBM3e good for 4 TB/s of memory bandwidth, and up to 4.6 petaFLOPS of FP4 compute. But we’ll note that it's in its 600 W configuration. When deployed in the Threadripper Halo, we expect AMD will be running the cards in the more sedate 450 W config. Combined, the Threadripper Halo promises up to 576 GB of HBM3e and 16 TB/s of memory bandwidth, enabling the system to run models exceeding a trillion parameters in size (at four-bit precision) entirely in GPU memory. By offloading some of the model to system memory, the system should be able to run the largest open weights models, like Moonshot.AI’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3. The ability to run large frontier-class models on your desk won’t come cheap and may not be available in every market, at least not without an electrical service upgrade. AMD hasn’t shared pricing, but as configured, we expect it to sell for somewhere between $100,000 and $150,000. A quad MI350P system is going to push the limits of a standard North American power outlet unless AMD either underclocks the cards from 600 W to 300 W or it mandates a 20 amp circuit. This might explain why the system AMD showed off at IFA only had two. At this price and power level, the system is well positioned to compete with Nvidia’s own high-end AI workstation, the DGX Station. Announced at GTC in 2025, the DGX Station features a 252 GB B300 GPU and a 72-core Grace CPU along with 496 GB of LPDDR5x memory, and it retails for around $100,000 if you can find one in stock. The House of Zen boasts that the system offers up to 3.4x the total system memory and more than twice the memory bandwidth of the DGX Station, which should give an edge in LLM inference, assuming tensor parallel operations don’t bottleneck on the CPU’s PCIe bus. AMD says the Threadripper Halo will be available starting next year. ®
